    Statistics for Psychology · Module 4

    Correlation

    Correlation is about how things go together.

    Two questions, always

    Which direction? Positive, negative, or none.

    How strong? Weak, moderate, or strong.

    This week

    • Direction and strength
    • The coefficient r
    • Benchmarks for interpreting it
    • Hypothesis testing with correlations
    • Correlation is not causation
    The rule everyone breaks

    Correlation is not causation. We'll spend real time on why.

    Before we start

    A quick revisit: confidence intervals

    A confidence interval says something about the population, based on your sample.

    Range includes zero

    Not significant. A CI of [−0.2, +0.2] contains zero — same as p ≥ .05.

    Range excludes zero

    Significant. Zero isn't in the range — same as p < .05.

    Useful in practice: even when a write-up prints no p value, the interval tells you whether the result was significant.

    Bigger n

    Narrower interval. Tighter range, less variability. What you want.

    Smaller n

    Wider interval. More variability. Normal for small samples, less informative.

    Say it like this

    “I am 95% confident that this is true of the population, based on the sample data.”

    The demo

    The Newlywed Game

    An old game show that turns out to be a nearly perfect analogy for correlation.

    Couples are asked questions about their partner, then we find out whether they got it right. Every week the show was effectively testing the relationship of married couples.

    Why it works

    Correlation is about relationships — how strong one is, and which direction it goes. That's what the show measures.

    Three kinds of couple

    Strong

    “We both said pizza!”

    They know each other extremely well.

    Weak

    “I said beach.” / “I said mountains.”

    Some agreement, but inconsistent.

    None

    “I said cats.” / “I said roller coasters.”

    Answers appear random.

    In-class activity

    Good, bad, or nowhere? And what evidence makes you say so?

    ↗ Positive

    Improving and getting stronger.

    → No clear

    Staying about the same.

    ↘ Negative

    Getting worse and becoming weaker.

    Foundations

    Correlation measures two things

    Strength

    How consistently do the two variables move together?

    Direction

    When one goes up, does the other go up, go down, or do nothing?

    And remember

    Correlation tells us how two variables move together. But correlation ≠ causation — more on that shortly.

    Direction

    Three directions

    We read graphs left to right — so just look at what the line is doing.

    Click a directionThen press play
    Cardi B — “Up”both variables go up
    Marvin Gaye — “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough”a high and a low
    Pink Floyd — “The Great Gig in the Sky”no words, just sound

    Positive

    As years of experience increase, income tends to increase.

    Negative

    As hours of exercise increase, weight tends to decrease.

    Zero

    How often you play a record has no relationship with your shoe size.

    Strength

    The correlation coefficient, r

    This is the value you look for in your output. It tells you how strong the relationship is.

    The scale

    r runs from −1 to +1. The closer to either end, the stronger the relationship. It can never go past 1 or −1.

    r = −1

    Perfect negative. Every dot on a line going down.

    r = 0

    No correlation. Dots everywhere.

    r = +1

    Perfect positive. Every dot on a line going up.

    Sign is direction, size is strength

    A negative r always means as one goes up the other goes down. The number tells you how much.

    The one to notice

    Anything at or beyond .40 or −.40 is a large effect. A lower bar than most people expect.

    Sort on the absolute value — r = −.35 and r = +.35 are equally strong, just opposite directions.

    Hypothesis testing

    Null and alternative, correlation edition

    Same George Costanza logic. Just do the opposite.

    H0 — Null

    There is no relationship, r = 0

    Assumes any correlation you saw is random chance.

    HA — Alternative

    There is a relationship, r ≠ 0

    Assumes a true relationship — positive or negative.

    The coffee example

    H0: There is no relationship between drinking coffee and productivity — r = 0.

    HA: There is a relationship — r ≠ 0.

    Still the same question

    To reject, or not to reject. A p under .05 lets you reject the null — but that's all it does. Direction and strength come from r.

    Putting it together

    What story is this telling you?

    Three things every time: direction, strength, and significance.

    Activity · Read the outputEach gives you an r and a p

    The hard cases are the interesting ones

    A significant result with a tiny r. A strong r that isn't significant. That's where you have to think rather than read an answer off the screen.

    Connecting back

    r versus Cohen's d

    Both are effect sizes. They measure different things — and you want opposite pictures from each.

    Cohen's d

    The difference between two group means. Picture two distributions — you're measuring the space between the peaks.

    You want the peaks far apart.

    Correlation, r

    The strength of a relationship. Picture a scatterplot — you're measuring how close the dots are to the line.

    You want the dots close to the line.

    Why opposite

    With d you're comparing two groups, so more separation means a bigger effect. With r you're asking how related two things are, so tighter clustering means a stronger relationship.

    Reading real results

    Two worked examples

    1 · Beer and publishing

    34 scientists. Beer consumed per year against likelihood of publishing.

    r = −.55, 95% CI [−.74, −.27]

    Direction

    Negative — the sign says so.

    Strength

    Large effect — past .40.

    The CI

    Wide — consistent with only 34 people.

    Notice the language

    “Associated with,” not “causes.” We are not saying beer causes fewer papers.

    2 · Exercise and positive emotions

    1,000 students across five universities.

    r = .32, CI [.29, .35]

    Direction

    Positive — more activity, more positive emotion.

    Strength

    Fairly powerful — the .30–.40 bucket.

    The CI

    Narrow — consistent with 1,000 people.

    The big one

    Correlation is not causation

    ▶

    Correlation and causation

    Short explainer

    Shorts, ice cream, and how one study's message degraded from paper to press release to headline.

    Watch ↗

    The classic

    People wearing shorts and ice cream sales are strongly related. Nobody thinks shorts cause ice cream. There's a common factor — warm weather.

    When can you claim causation?

    Only from an experiment, where you randomly allocate people to conditions. Most studies are observational — we look and measure, so we can only say two things are linked.

    How it goes wrong

    The paper said

    “We observed consistent associations between higher socio-economic position and higher risk of glioma.”

    The press release said

    “High levels of education are linked to heightened brain tumour risk.” — though the study wasn't about education.

    The headline said

    “Why going to university increases the risk of getting a brain tumour.”

    The authors' own explanation: wealthier people get better healthcare, so they're more likely to be diagnosed.

    Back to the Newlywed Game

    A couple answers everything right. All we know is they have a strong relationship. We don't know why — ten years together first? Therapy? The correlation can't tell us.

    One more

    Is there a relationship between living in the northeast and snowfall? Probably. Does living there cause snow? No — weather does.

    Language

    Watch your verbs

    Rule of thumb

    Observational study → association verbs only. Experiment → you've earned a causal verb.

    Activity · Which kind of claim?Click a verb, then a column

    A wrinkle

    Correlations don't really have an IV and a DV

    You're not manipulating anything — just two variables and a question about how they move together.

    But for your final paper

    You may have framed your variables as IV and DV — cups of coffee, productivity on a 1–10 scale. You can absolutely still run a correlation. Just describe the result as a relationship, not an effect.

    4 · Interpret

    Why it matters beyond the assignment

    People may only read your abstract. They may only look at your tables. Assume someone will look at exactly one thing — and build your tables accordingly.

    A note on the word “hypothesis”

    In these papers “hypothesis” usually just means a prediction. That's not the same as hypothesis testing, which means testing the null. Same word, two jobs.

    Wrapping up

    What to take away

    Direction

    The sign of r. Negative means as one goes up the other goes down. Look at the line.

    Strength

    The size of r. How close are the dots to the line? Past .40 is a large effect.
